beats.title: The Question
beats.narration_text: Hi. This is Sanjiv. Today we shall discuss how a machine breaks down language with tokenization. You write a sentence. A language model receives numbers. Tokenization connects those two worlds. Let us follow the conversion, build a tiny tokenizer, and see why a token is not the same thing as a word.

props.command: Explain tokenization: split text into pieces, build a tiny tokenizer, and compare tokens with words.
output: IDs → connect pieces to model input

beats.title: The Whole Idea
beats.narration_text: Tokenization divides text into units and assigns each unit an identifier from a vocabulary. Those units can be words, parts of words, or smaller pieces. The choice changes how text is represented. It does not, by itself, give the machine an understanding of language.

props.text:
Tokenization understands language
as pieces and numeric IDs.

beats.title: Choose the Pieces
beats.narration_text: Here are three ways to package cats. Keep the whole word, split every character, or reuse a piece such as cat and a piece such as s. Whole words need many vocabulary entries. Characters produce longer sequences. Subwords offer a compromise. These splits are illustrations, not claims about a particular model.

shot.visual_intent: Show “cats” once. Three successive panels: whole word [cats]; characters [c][a][t][s]; illustrative subwords [cat][s]. Never show all three panels together.

beats.title: Learn a Merge
beats.narration_text: Our tiny training collection contains low five times and lower twice. We start with characters and count neighboring pairs across that collection. L followed by o occurs seven times. So does o followed by w. That is a tie. Our example resolves ties alphabetically, so l and o merge first.

beats.title: Merge Again
beats.narration_text: Now count again using the updated pieces. Lo followed by w appears seven times, so it becomes low. This is the central move in byte-pair encoding: repeatedly merge a frequent adjacent pair. We stop after two merges to keep the example visible. Real vocabularies keep far more pieces.

shot.visual_intent: Tile boundaries join: [l][o][w] → [lo][w]. Then [lo][w] → [low]. Labels are whole strings throughout; use panel swaps and boundary motion, never letter replacement animations.

beats.title: Apply the Rules
beats.narration_text: Training learned the rules. Encoding applies those saved rules to an input. Lower starts as characters, then the two learned merges produce low, e, and r. Each piece has an ID in our toy vocabulary. Another tokenizer can split this same word differently and assign completely different IDs.

shot.visual_intent: Restore text → pieces → IDs framework. Process “lower” with learned rules into [low][e][r], then IDs from the executed toy vocabulary. Label “Toy tokenizer” beside the graphic.

beats.title: IDs Are Addresses
beats.narration_text: An ID is a lookup address. It is not a definition, a score, or a measure of similarity. The model uses those IDs to retrieve learned vectors called embeddings. The tokenizer supplies the sequence. The model processes its representations in context. Keep those jobs separate.

shot.visual_intent: Three token cards above three ID boxes. Arrow to a small embedding lookup table. Numeric vectors are abstract colored cells, labeled “learned vectors”; no invented semantic axes.

beats.title: Break the Toy
beats.narration_text: Now change the first letter to a capital. Our tiny vocabulary has no capital L, so this toy tokenizer fails there. Byte-level designs can start with all possible byte values instead. A character can occupy more than one byte. That helps represent unfamiliar text, but representing it is not the same as understanding it.

beats.title: Test the Boundary
beats.narration_text: When inspecting a real model, use its matching tokenizer. Compare lowercase and uppercase text, then add a leading space. Inspect the actual pieces and IDs instead of guessing them. Normalization and whitespace handling are part of the pipeline, so you should also check what survives decoding.

shot.visual_intent: One comparison at a time: “lower” versus “Lower”, then “lower” versus “ lower”. Show inspection checklist: tokenizer name, exact input, pieces and IDs. No fabricated model outputs.

beats.title: The Takeaway
beats.narration_text: The useful habit is to inspect the encoding. Do not assume one word means one token, or that token boundaries follow grammar. Save the tokenizer identity with your experiment. Then a surprising split becomes something you can reproduce and investigate, instead of a mystery about how the machine reads.

artifactLines: PIECES — a token need not be a word.
IDENTITY — save the tokenizer with the experiment.
DECODE — compare with the original text.
